items.title: Flood Frequency Reduction Measures (45,000 cfs / 100-year target)
items.operational_question: What flood-frequency-reduction commitment governs unanticipated floods exceeding 45,000 cfs at Glen Canyon Dam, and how is it achieved?
items.consolidated_finding: Under the 1996 ROD's Flood Frequency Reduction Measures, the frequency of unanticipated floods exceeding 45,000 cfs is to be reduced to an average of once in 100 years, accomplished initially through the Annual Operating Plan process and eventually by raising Glen Canyon Dam's spillway gates 4.5 feet (EU-LP-OFF-008-05). The 2002 Report to Congress restates the identical commitment: the frequency of unanticipated flood flows exceeding 45,000 cfs will be reduced to no more than 1 year in 100 years as a long-term average, using the same two-phase approach -- Annual Operating Plan process, then a 4.5-foot spillway gate raise (EU-LP-OFF-009-07).

items.title: Conditions for Exceeding the 25,000 cfs Release Cap
items.operational_question: Under what conditions may Glen Canyon Dam exceed the normal 25,000 cfs maximum release limit?
items.consolidated_finding: Under the 2016 LTEMP FEIS, when very wet hydrologic conditions occur (average monthly release rate above 25,000 cfs), Glen Canyon Dam may exceed the 25,000 cfs cap but must release at a constant rate; the limit may also be exceeded to avoid spills, during flood releases, for approved experimental high-flow-experiment (HFE) releases, or to accommodate electrical emergencies (EU-LP-OFF-005-06). Consistent with this, the 2007 Biological Assessment states the 25,000 cfs maximum flow limit under the 1996 ROD and 1997 Operating Criteria may be exceeded for emergency conditions and during extreme hydrological conditions, and notes that separate emergency exception criteria also apply during normal operations (EU-LP-OFF-011-16).
items.source_coverage_note: The 2016 LTEMP FEIS gives a specific enumerated list of exceedance conditions (wet hydrology, spills, floods, HFEs, electrical emergencies); the 2007 Biological Assessment gives a more general emergency/extreme-hydrology framing of the same rule. Read together they give a fuller picture than either alone.

items.title: Glen Canyon Dam Emergency Exception Criteria
items.operational_question: What are the Emergency Exception Criteria that allow Glen Canyon Dam to deviate from normal operating rules during emergencies, and what situations do they cover?
items.consolidated_finding: The Emergency Exception Criteria were established under Section 3 of the Glen Canyon Dam Operating Criteria (62 FR 9448, March 3, 1997) and continue unchanged under LTEMP Alternative D; when invoked, normal operations are suspended until the emergency has ended or WAPA has discharged its NERC responsibility regarding the emergency (EU-LP-OFF-003-09). The 1996 ROD establishes that these criteria allow WAPA to respond to various emergency situations consistent with its North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC) obligations, with exceptions to standard operating criteria during search-and-rescue situations, special studies and monitoring, dam and powerplant maintenance, and spinning reserves (EU-LP-OFF-008-06). GAO's 1997 assessment describes these deviations as usually lasting less than 4 hours, covering power and water emergencies such as insufficient generating capacity, restoration of the electrical system, or search-and-rescue operations (EU-LP-OFF-010-05). The underlying NERC standard requires a disturbance (sudden generation loss or transmission imbalance) be corrected within 10 minutes; Glen Canyon Dam's reserve capacity is also contractually used to restart tripped thermal powerplants and provide emergency shutdown power to nuclear powerplants, and responding to such electrical emergencies is exempt from 1996 ROD operating constraints (EU-LP-OFF-005-11).
items.source_coverage_note: Four documents (1996 ROD, 1997 GAO report, 2016 LTEMP ROD, 2016 LTEMP FEIS Chapter 3) describe the same Emergency Exception Criteria instrument from different angles -- legal citation and continuity, WAPA/NERC scope, typical duration, and the specific NERC 10-minute correction standard -- no single document gives the complete picture.

items.title: DROA 3,525-ft Protective Elevation Target
items.operational_question: What is the Drought Response Operations Agreement's (DROA) protective elevation target for Lake Powell, and how is it triggered and implemented?
items.consolidated_finding: Under the Upper Basin DCP's DROA, Upper Basin states agreed to operate system units to keep Lake Powell's surface above elevation 3,525 feet, 35 feet above minimum power pool (EU-LP-CRS-001-04). Reclamation's stated operational goal under DROA is to 'protect' this 3,525-ft elevation, primarily via reduced Glen Canyon Dam releases and drawdown of upstream initial-unit reservoirs (EU-LP-CRS-002-04). The DROA establishes the process for Reclamation, in collaboration with the Upper Basin States, to release additional water from upstream CRSP initial-unit reservoirs (Flaming Gorge, Aspinall, Navajo, Glen Canyon/Lake Powell) to reduce the risk of Lake Powell reaching critical elevation (EU-LP-OFF-017-03). In CRSS modeling, Powell Infrastructure Protection (PIP) releases from the Upper Initial Units (Flaming Gorge, Blue Mesa, Navajo) are specifically triggered when Lake Powell is projected to fall below elevation 3,525 feet (EU-LP-OFF-021-06). This target was actually invoked when the July 2025 24-Month Study projected Lake Powell declining below the 3,525.00-ft DROA target elevation, triggering DROA year-2025 drought-response planning under the DCP-related agreements (EU-LP-OFF-022-03); consistent with protecting this same target, the December 2025 24-Month Study reduced Glen Canyon Dam's monthly release volumes for December 2025 through April 2026 by 0.598 maf (EU-LP-OFF-023-03).
items.source_coverage_note: Six sources spanning CRS reports, the DROA program page, CRSS model documentation, and the 2025-2026 Annual Operating Plan/24-Month Study data converge on the same 3,525-ft target and mechanism, moving from policy description to an actual 2025-2026 real-time invocation. One EU (EU-LP-OFF-023-03) carries a source dimension tag of Real-Time Operations rather than Emergency Operations; it is included here because it documents the same emergency elevation-protection mechanism as the other five EUs.

items.title: 2026 Emergency Drought Response (Flaming Gorge Release and Release Reduction)
items.operational_question: What emergency drought-response actions did Reclamation take in 2026 to protect Lake Powell from falling to critically low elevation?
items.consolidated_finding: On April 17, 2026, the Bureau of Reclamation announced unprecedented actions to store more water in Lake Powell -- then less than 25 percent full -- to preserve hydropower generation and protect Glen Canyon Dam water-delivery infrastructure the agency said was at risk from low reservoir levels (EU-LP-MED-001-01). With the consent of the four Upper Basin states, Reclamation committed to releasing between 660,000 and 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge Reservoir (82 percent full) into Lake Powell over the 12 months following the announcement, building on a smaller 463,000-acre-foot release used to prop up Powell in 2022-23 (EU-LP-MED-001-02). Because WY2026 was historically dry and Lake Powell was projected to decline below elevation 3,500 feet, the Department of the Interior invoked Section 6.E of the 2024 Interim Guidelines SEIS ROD to reduce Lake Powell's annual release from 7.48 maf to 6.00 maf, coupled with a 2026 Drought Response Operations Plan releasing approximately 660,000 to 1.00 maf of additional water from Flaming Gorge Reservoir to Lake Powell by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-023-02). Reclamation's newsroom release confirms the combined plan: adding about 2.48 million acre-feet via the 660,000 AF-1 maf Flaming Gorge release (April 2026-April 2027, under the 2019 Drought Response Operating Agreements) plus the 7.48-to-6.0-maf release reduction through September 2026 under Section 6E, together expected to raise Lake Powell's elevation about 54 feet to at least 3,500 feet by April 2027 (EU-LP-OFF-035-02).

items.title: 2026 Lake Mead Shortage Condition and State Contributions

items.title: Post-2012 High-Flow Experiment Protocol
items.operational_question: What is the Glen Canyon Dam high-flow-experiment (HFE) protocol established since 2012, and what triggers its implementation?
items.consolidated_finding: High flow experiments were tested in 1996, 1997, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2014 to rebuild eroded sandbars; since 2012 a 10-year protocol implements one to two high flow experiments annually, timed to follow tributary sand inputs from the Paria River in fall and/or spring (EU-LP-RES-014-05). This decision-making protocol, approved by the Department of the Interior in 2012, coordinates dam releases to occur following large sand inputs delivered to the Colorado River by a major tributary (EU-LP-RES-018-01). Across the full historical record, 11 HFEs were released from Glen Canyon Dam between 1996 and November 2018, with peak magnitudes ranging from 864 to 1,274 cubic meters per second and durations from 24 to 168 hours, including lower-magnitude habitat maintenance flows (HMFs) in 1997 and 2000 (EU-LP-RES-018-02).

EU-LP-RES-014-05 carries a source dimension tag of Real-Time Operations while the other two are tagged Emergency Operations; Emergency Operations is used here consistent with how HFEs are tagged elsewhere in this corpus.

items.title: 1996 First Controlled-Flood Experiment
items.operational_question: What were the specifics and outcome of the 1996 Glen Canyon Dam controlled-flood (first HFE) experiment?
items.consolidated_finding: In spring 1996 Reclamation conducted its first controlled-flood (beach/habitat-building) experiment, ramping releases from a steady 8,000 cfs baseline up to a peak of 45,000 cfs (approximately 1,274 cubic meters per second) held for 7 days beginning March 26, 1996, before stepping back down; preliminary results showed sandbars in the Glen and Grand canyons increased by as much as 30 percent and numerous new backwaters were created for fish (EU-LP-OFF-010-14). The 1996 HFE's major objective was to determine whether high releases from Glen Canyon Dam could effectively redistribute sand from the riverbed to the channel margins; because it followed two years of below-average tributary sand input, suspended sediment progressively coarsened and depleted during the event (EU-LP-RES-018-08).
items.source_coverage_note: A 1997 GAO report gives the release hydrograph and immediate sandbar/backwater results; a 2018 USGS research paper gives the experiment's stated objective and the antecedent sediment-supply context that constrained its outcome. Source dimension tags differ (EU-LP-OFF-010-14 tagged Real-Time Operations; EU-LP-RES-018-08 tagged Emergency Operations); Emergency Operations is used here consistent with HFE tagging elsewhere.

items.title: Non-Native Fish Suppression Flows (2003-2005)
items.operational_question: What non-native fish suppression flow pattern was implemented at Glen Canyon Dam during 2003-2005, and what were its parameters?
items.consolidated_finding: As part of the 2002-2004 experimental program, Reclamation implemented non-native fish suppression releases from Glen Canyon Dam with daily fluctuations of 5,000-20,000 cfs during January 1-March 31 of 2003, continuing this high-fluctuation suppression flow pattern in 2004 and 2005 to test its effectiveness at limiting non-native fish recruitment (EU-LP-OFF-011-14). items.title: Glen Canyon Dam Design Flood and Flood Routing
items.operational_question: What was Glen Canyon Dam's original design flood, and how was reservoir storage used to reduce the required spillway discharge?
items.consolidated_finding: Glen Canyon Dam's spillways were designed to pass a maximum probable snowmelt flood with a predicted peak discharge of 380,000 cfs and a volume of 29,060,000 acre-feet over a 4-month period, about 1.7 times the maximum recorded historical discharge of 220,000 cfs (EU-LP-OFF-027-05). items.title: River Outlet Works: Capacity, History, and Reliability Risk
items.operational_question: What are Glen Canyon Dam's River Outlet Works, what is their release capacity, and what is known about their historical use and reliability?
items.consolidated_finding: The River Outlet Works (bypass tubes) have historically only been opened when the dam was first filled, during short-term high-flow experiments, and for emergency flood releases in the early 1980s, and have never been used over extended periods (EU-LP-CRS-002-03). Below minimum power pool, the River Outlet Works are the only remaining way to pass water through Glen Canyon Dam: two intakes leading to four 96-inch-diameter steel pipes with a combined maximum discharge capacity of 15,000 cubic feet per second (EU-LP-MED-002-02), a capacity figure confirmed on Reclamation's own project page, which also lists a combined spillway discharge capacity of 208,000 cfs at elevation 3,700.0 ft (EU-LP-OFF-030-02). Since the Draft SEIS, Reclamation identified enhanced risks associated with relying on the River Outlet Works as the exclusive means of releasing water at low reservoir elevations for sustained periods, prompting the 2024 Interim Operating Guidance for Low Reservoir Levels (EU-LP-OFF-007-04).
items.source_coverage_note: A CRS report, a journalism piece, a 2024 SEIS chapter, and Reclamation's own project page together establish the River Outlet Works' physical capacity, historically limited/short-duration use, and an emerging (2024) agency concern about relying on them for sustained low-elevation operation.

items.operational_question: What flow magnitude, physical release pathway, and duration define a High-Flow Experiment (HFE) release from Glen Canyon Dam?
items.consolidated_finding: High-Flow Experiment (HFE) releases from Glen Canyon Dam are triggered when there is sufficient sediment input from the Paria River and typically range from approximately 30,000 to 45,000 cfs, used to mobilize channel-stored sand and redeposit it as sandbars, beaches, and associated backwater/riparian habitat. items.title: Release-Capacity Loss Below Minimum Power Pool (3,490 ft)
items.operational_question: What operational constraint does Glen Canyon Dam face when Lake Powell falls below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, and what release-capacity shortfall results?
items.consolidated_finding: When Lake Powell drops below the minimum power pool elevation of 3,490 feet, Glen Canyon Dam can no longer release water through its powerplant turbines/penstocks and must rely on the river outlet works (ROW), whose capacity is limited and increases with pool elevation (OFF-021-08); the Post-2026 Draft EIS states the dam 'was not envisioned to operate below minimum power pool (elevation 3,490 feet)' and that below this elevation water must be released through the jet tubes at the end of the ROW instead of the penstocks (OFF-019-05). items.title: Reliability Risk of the River Outlet Works as a Long-Term Release Path
items.operational_question: Can the river outlet works (ROW) reliably serve as the sole long-term release mechanism for Glen Canyon Dam at low Lake Powell reservoir levels?
items.consolidated_finding: Multiple sources indicate the river outlet works (ROW) were not designed for, and cannot be fully relied upon for, long-term or high-flow releases at low Lake Powell levels. Reclamation's 2024 Technical Decision Memorandum found no design reference indicating the ROW were intended for long-term water conveyance at low reservoir levels; historically they were used only to augment powerplant/spillway discharges for short durations (e.g., about three months during 1983 flood releases, days to a week for high-flow experiments) (OFF-025-04). A 2023 special inspection found the hollow-jet valves, pipes, and ring-follower gates sufficient for periodic/seasonal releases but flagged concern about long-term high-flow use and recommended a major overhaul or replacement for high confidence in continuous long-term operation (OFF-025-05). This concern has historical precedent: on April 20, 1965, at reservoir elevation 3,490 ft with the ROW variably open, the dam's tailrace stabilization slab was undermined by a recirculating eddy from ROW operation and portions of it collapsed, because tailwater was 4-6 feet lower than had been predicted by physical modeling (OFF-025-06). More recently, in 2023, when the ROW were used for a high-flow release into the Grand Canyon at low-reservoir levels, damaging cavitation occurred, and the Bureau has warned further extended use would likely cause more (MED-002-03). Based on this evidence, Reclamation's formal conclusion is that it should not rely on the ROW as the sole means of releasing water from Glen Canyon Dam, as would be required below minimum power pool (3,490 ft), given current uncertainty about long-term conduit and hollow-jet valve performance and tailrace sedimentation (OFF-025-07).

items.title: Lake Mead 1,000-Foot Elevation as a Basin Risk Threshold
items.operational_question: What significance does the Lake Mead elevation of 1,000 feet hold as a basin-wide risk/vulnerability threshold in Colorado River operations?
items.consolidated_finding: A Lake Mead elevation of 1,000 feet functions as a recurring basin-wide risk/vulnerability threshold in Colorado River risk management. The 2007 Interim Guidelines ROD establishes a mandatory annual consultation requirement: whenever Lake Mead is below elevation 1,025 feet, the Secretary must consult with the Basin States on whether hydrologic conditions and anticipated deliveries are likely to cause Lake Mead to fall below 1,000 feet, and must implement any additional measures consistent with applicable federal law (OFF-001-09). Separately, the 2016 SECURE Water Act report describes the Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study's use of Lake Mead elevation dropping below 1,000 feet in any month as one of two defined system-reliability vulnerability metrics (the other being a 'Lee Ferry deficit,' when the 10-year running total flow at Lee Ferry falls below 75 MAF) (OFF-018-04).

items.title: Economic Impact of 1996 ROD MLFF Operating Restrictions
items.operational_question: What economic and operational impact did the 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) restrictions have on Glen Canyon Dam hydropower operations?
items.consolidated_finding: The 1996 ROD's Modified Low Fluctuating Flow (MLFF) operating criteria reduced Glen Canyon Dam powerplant's operating flexibility and, consequently, its economic value. items.title: Storage-Driven Release Warming and Nonnative-Fish Predation Risk to Humpback Chub
items.operational_question: What risk does warmer Glen Canyon Dam releases, caused by reduced Lake Powell storage, pose to humpback chub via nonnative-fish predation and competition?
items.consolidated_finding: Reduced Lake Powell storage, by warming Glen Canyon Dam releases, has been identified as a risk pathway for increased nonnative-fish predation and competition pressure on humpback chub. River warming that occurred from 2003 to 2011 (and again in 2014), resulting from reduced Lake Powell storage, was intended to benefit native humpback chub, but the Grand Canyon Ecosystem Model predicted that nonnative fish would also benefit, potentially increasing predation/competition risk to humpback chub through greater fish interactions in critical river segments (RES-014-06). Consistent with this risk pathway, the 2008 Final Biological Opinion notes that because prolonged droughts (paleoclimate tree-ring records show droughts of 15-20 years) could lower Lake Powell storage and raise dam release temperatures, increasing nonnative predation risk to humpback chub, Reclamation committed to monitor and control nonnative fish as necessary through the Adaptive Management Program if such warming occurs (OFF-012-18).

items.title: EVPI-Based Sensitivity of LTEMP Strategy Ranking to Scientific Uncertainty
items.operational_question: How sensitive was the LTEMP preferred long-term operating strategy to the critical scientific/system uncertainties evaluated in the supporting decision analysis?
items.consolidated_finding: A decision analysis supporting LTEMP development found that the ranking of preferred long-term operating strategies was not sensitive to the critical scientific/system uncertainties evaluated (trout-humpback chub dynamics, trout-management-flow effectiveness, HFE effects on trout), but was sensitive mainly to stakeholders' value-based weighting of resource goals, with long-term hydrological input pattern being the one uncertainty that slightly affected rankings (RES-024-02). This was assessed using the expected value of perfect information (EVPI), which sets an upper bound on the value of experimental or adaptive management by comparing expected performance under uncertainty to expected performance if uncertainty could be fully resolved before a decision, and the related expected value of partial information (EVXI), which evaluates the value of resolving only part of the uncertainty (RES-024-07). The quantitative result: EVPI for the critical scientific uncertainties (fall HFE effect on trout, trout-management-flow effectiveness, temperature-versus-trout effect on humpback chub) was essentially zero for nearly all stakeholder weightings -- the same best-performing long-term strategy was identified across all 16 combinations of competing hypotheses for 12 of 14 stakeholders, and the two exceptions had an EVPI of less than 0.1 percent (RES-024-17).

items.title: September 2005 Dissolved Oxygen Violation at Glen Canyon Dam
items.operational_question: What operational failure occurred with dissolved oxygen in Glen Canyon Dam releases in September 2005, and what caused it?
items.consolidated_finding: In fall 2005, a plume of oxygen-depleted water in Lake Powell was captured in the penstock withdrawal zone and exported through Glen Canyon Dam, dropping tailwater dissolved oxygen below 4.0 mg/L in September 2005 and violating EPA cold-water fishery DO criteria (1-day mean minimum 4.0 mg/L, 7-day mean minimum 5.0 mg/L, 30-day mean 6.5 mg/L) (RES-020-02). items.title: Early Sediment-Redistribution Flow Tests (1997, 2000) Failed to Build Sandbars
items.operational_question: What early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, and why?
items.consolidated_finding: Two early post-dam sediment-redistribution flow experiments, predating the LTEMP HFE protocol, failed to achieve their sandbar-building objectives, each for a different reason. The November 3, 1997 Test Flow (a constant 872 m3/s release for 48 hours), Reclamation's first attempt at a post-tributary-flood sediment-redistribution release, did not significantly aggrade sandbars because its magnitude was insufficient to distribute sand to open depositional locations at higher elevations (RES-018-09). The 2000 Low Summer Steady Flow Experiment (a 4-day 864 m3/s release, 3 months of constant 227 m3/s, then a 4-day 881 m3/s release) produced minimal sandbar building because the Paria River had supplied very little sediment beforehand, and the sustained low, steady discharge instead allowed proliferation of invasive tamarisk seedlings on bare sand deposits (RES-018-10).
items.source_coverage_note: Both EUs are from the same 2022 USGS sandbar-response paper, describing sequential early experimental flow releases (1997 and 2000) that share the same objective (sandbar aggradation) but failed for different documented reasons (insufficient magnitude vs. insufficient sediment supply).

items.title: Long-Term HFE Effectiveness Varies by Sandbar Type
items.operational_question: What has been the long-term effectiveness of the High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol at rebuilding different types of Grand Canyon sandbars?
items.consolidated_finding: The long-term effectiveness of the High-Flow Experiment (HFE) protocol at rebuilding Grand Canyon sandbars differs by bar type and has structural limits at both ends. At wide reattachment bars and upper pool deposits, vegetation stabilization and vertical aggradation during successive HFEs have progressively narrowed the channel and reduced the accommodation space available for further deposition, so at best HFEs can only replace sediment eroded during normal dam operations between events rather than produce net growth (RES-018-12). At separation bars and undifferentiated eddy bars, HFEs have not effectively rebuilt the bars, which have continued to gradually decrease in volume over time; although these bars consistently aggrade during individual HFEs, the subsequent erosion at these unvegetated, wind-exposed sites is rapid (RES-018-13).
